messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 24-year-old South Asian diplomat, has been struggling since his traumatic experience in a war-torn region. The event that deeply shook him occurred when he was caught in an explosion while on assignment. Though physically unharmed, the emotional and psychological toll of that day has left lasting scars. Even now, Ravi cannot shake the feeling of vulnerability that haunts him. Any hint of alcohol or the sound of a sudden bang sends him spiraling back to that moment when everything felt out of control. The smell of alcohol often brings him back to the aftermath, where soldiers and civilians alike drank heavily in an attempt to cope with their own trauma. These triggers have led Ravi to adopt several maladaptive strategies. He has taken to using drugs as a means to numb his heightened emotions and intrusive memories. He also pushes himself to exercise excessively, hoping that physical exhaustion might provide some respite from the relentless thoughts about the event. Wearing concealing clothing helps him feel slightly more protected, but it does little to quell the constant fear. The sense of vulnerability is not just emotional; Ravi feels constantly threatened by his surroundings. Even when others tell him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them. He frequently experiences flashbacks where he feels as though the explosion is happening again. This only deepens his mistrust and makes every stranger approaching him feel like a potential threat. Ravi's memories of that day are vivid and detailed. He can clearly recall the smell of smoke and burning rubber, which often resurfaces when he encounters similar scents. The clarity of these memories has left Ravi struggling to find words to describe his experience, but they remain etched in his mind, a constant reminder of what he went through. The trauma has also led Ravi to question everything about himself and the world around him. He believes there is something inherently wrong with him that made him a target for such an event. This loss of faith extends beyond just himself; he no longer trusts people or life itself. The feeling of hopelessness weighs heavily on him, making it difficult to envision any future. These negative appraisals have further fueled his maladaptive behaviors and heightened sense of threat. His drug use has become a desperate attempt to escape the intrusive memories that plague him. Every time he exercises excessively, it is an effort to maintain control over something in his life that feels so out of reach. The cycle continues to tighten around Ravi. The more vivid his memories become, the greater his sense of threat grows. This leads to more frequent drug use and compulsive exercise as coping mechanisms. His loss of faith reinforces these behaviors, creating a self-reinforcing loop where each component feeds into the next. Despite his efforts to manage his symptoms, they have taken a toll on Ravi's personal and professional life. He has become increasingly isolated from his partner, and his work performance has suffered due to frequent absences and difficulty concentrating. The constant fear and flashbacks have made it nearly impossible for him to function normally in his role as a diplomat. What finally brought Ravi to seek help was the realization that he could no longer carry this burden alone. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again, of being trapped in a perpetual state of hypervigilance. At the same time, he hopes for a future where he can reclaim some sense of normalcy and trust in himself and others. Ravi's journey has been one of gradual deterioration, with each layer of trauma reinforcing the next. The complex interplay between his triggers, maladaptive strategies, perceptions of threat, memory intrusions, and negative appraisals forms a tight knot that he is only now beginning to unravel.
